newsitem.title: SWITZERLAND: EU, U.S. face off at world trade body over Cuba.
newsitem.headline: EU, U.S. face off at world trade body over Cuba.

text.p: The European Union, brushing aside objections from the United States, on Wednesday won agreement in the World Trade Organisation for a dispute panel to decide if the U.S. Helms-Burton law on Cuba runs against open trade rules.

U.S. officials immediately warned the EU decision to go ahead with the case could endanger the two-year-old WTO and indicated they would invoke national security in defence of the law which has been widely condemned around the world.

Accord in the WTO's Dispute Settlement Body (DSB) on creation of a panel of three neutral trade experts, expected to return their findings by mid-1997, was automatic once the EU said it wanted to go ahead.

Brussels trade envoy Ian Wilkinson told the DSB that though the 15-nation Union did not contest the official aim of the law -- to bring democracy to communist-ruled Cuba -- the EU could not accept its effect on other powers' trade with the island.

"The fundamental objectives of the U.S. legislation are not in dispute. But we have serious trade impairment, and there is also the question of extra-territoriality to be considered," he told reporters after the DSB session.
"So we are pursuing the dispute settlement mechanism in an orthodox and quiet way."

Critics of the Helms-Burton act, signed by President Bill Clinton in February after Cuba shot down two planes flown by Miami-based exiles near the island, say it aims to extend the reach of U.S. law to states trading with and investing in Cuba.

It gives U.S. citizens, including naturalised Cubans, the right to sue foreign companies that own or operate properties seized by the government of Fidel Castro after his guerrillas overthrew a right-wing dictatorial regime in 1959.

But it also provides for the barring from the United States of executives of companies investing in nationalised property in Cuba, and incorporates parts of earlier U.S. anti-Castro legislation aimed at isolating the island, under U.S. economic sanctions for over three decades.

Parts of the law have been suspended until early next year, but businesses in Canada and Mexico -- which are pursuing action under their North American Free Trade (NAFTA) accord with the United States -- and in Europe have already been affected.

In remarks to the DSB, on which all 125 members of the WTO can sit, U.S. ambassador Booth Gardner argued that the problem was not a trade matter and was linked to Washington foreign and security policy with regard to Cuba.
"We do not believe that recourse to a WTO panel will lead to a resolution of this dispute," he declared.
"On the other hand, we do believe that proceeding further with this matter would pose serious risks for this new and invaluable organisation, which is at the early stages of its development."

His remarks appeared to reflect concern that if a panel found against the U.S. position and rejected the claim to a "national security" opt-out from WTO rules, Congressional dislike and suspicion of the trade body could be hardened.

But other trade envoys have argued that if Washington were allowed to break the rules on national security grounds, it could open the floodgates to similar action by other countries and undermine the coherence of the WTO.
Cuba's WTO ambassador Eumelio Caballero Rodriguez told the DSB that he objected strongly to the U.S. argument.
"Cuba has never occupied nor invaded any part of U.S. territory, nor sponsored terrorist groups to act against the United States from its soil, as the U.S. has done," he said.
"It is our country which should be speaking of the threat to national sovereignty."
